topic.name: Women's Health: Contraception & Menopause
objectives: Compare contraceptive methods using efficacy rates and patient-specific factors
Diagnose and manage menopausal symptoms with hormonal and non-hormonal therapies
Identify and treat common causes of vaginitis using Amsel's criteria and microscopy
Interpret abnormal Pap smears and manage according to ASCCP guidelines

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Maria, 24, comes in saying she 'doesn't want to be on the pill' because it made her gain weight and feel moody. Her sister just had an IUD placed and loves it, but Maria heard 'it can perforate your uterus.' She's sexually active with one partner and wants something 'set it and forget it.' Every day in primary care, you'll help patients navigate these choices — and getting it right means preventing unintended pregnancy AND keeping them coming back for care.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision tree showing patient preferences branching to different contraceptive options with efficacy rates

content_chunks.title: Contraceptive Efficacy: The Tier System
content_chunks.content:
**CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC)** categorizes methods by **typical-use efficacy**:

**Tier 1 — Most Effective (>99%)**:
• **LARC (Long-Acting Reversible Contraception)** — IUDs (Mirena, Paragard, Kyleena, Liletta) and implant (Nexplanon)
• **Sterilization** — tubal ligation, vasectomy
• Failure rate: <1 per 100 woman-years

**Tier 2 — Effective (91-94%)**:
• **Oral contraceptive pills** (COCs + POPs)
• **Contraceptive patch** (Xulane, Twirla)
• **Vaginal ring** (NuvaRing, Annovera)
• **DMPA injection** (Depo-Provera)

**Tier 3 — Less Effective (72-88%)**:
• **Condoms** (male + female)
• **Diaphragm**, **cervical cap**, **sponge**
• **Withdrawal**, **rhythm method**

**Key Point**: LARC has HIGHEST satisfaction and continuation rates. ACOG recommends LARC as first-line for MOST adolescents and women.
content_chunks.mnemonic: **LARC First**: **L**ong-**A**cting **R**eversible **C**ontraception = **L**owest failure, **A**ll ages, **R**eally effective, **C**ost-effective over time
content_chunks.visual_desc: Pyramid graphic with tiers — Tier 1 (LARC/sterilization) at top with >99%, Tier 2 (pills/patch/ring/DMPA) with 91-94%, Tier 3 (condoms/barrier) with 72-88%

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **LARC myths debunked**: IUDs do NOT cause infertility, pelvic infection (except at insertion if active STI), or perforation (risk 1/1000, usually at insertion). Nexplanon insertion/removal is faster than a Pap smear. **Mirena is FDA-approved for heavy menstrual bleeding** — a two-for-one win in perimenopausal patients.

content_chunks.title: Quick-Start Contraception Protocol
content_chunks.content:
**Quick-Start** — start hormones the day of visit (no need to wait for menses) IF:
• Reasonably certain not pregnant (no recent unprotected sex, no signs of pregnancy)
• **Urine pregnancy test negative** (obtain first!)
• If started >5 days after menses onset → use backup (condoms) for 7 days

**IUD Insertion Checklist**:
✅ CBC if heavy menses
✅ **Chlamydia/gonorrhea screening** (treat before insertion if positive)
✅ Bimanual exam to determine uterine position
✅ Insert during menses for easier cervix (optional, can do anytime)
✅ Counsel on expected cramping/spotting for 1-3 months
✅ Ultrasound guidance if difficult insertion or uncertain position

**When to REFER**: Uterine anomaly, recent postpartum <4 weeks, active PID, cervical or endometrial cancer
content_chunks.visual_desc: Flowchart: Patient wants contraception → Pregnancy test → Negative → Assess preferences → Choose method → If LARC: STI screening → Insert → Follow-up in 4-6 weeks

quick_checks.q: Which contraceptive method has the HIGHEST typical-use efficacy and continuation rate?
quick_checks.explanation: LARC methods have >99% efficacy and highest satisfaction + continuation rates per ACOG. Pills have 91% typical use and high discontinuation due to daily adherence.

quick_checks.q: A 19-year-old wants IUD placement. What MUST you do first?
answers: Wait until she has had a child
quick_checks.explanation: Screen for STIs before IUD insertion. If positive, treat first. Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended. Nulliparity is NOT a contraindication to IUDs.

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Susan, 52, hasn't slept through the night in 6 months. She wakes up drenched in sweat, her mood is unpredictable ('my family walks on eggshells'), and she's gaining weight around her middle despite no change in diet. Her mother had a 'really bad menopause' and Susan says, 'I guess I just have to suffer through it like she did.' She doesn't — and neither do your patients. Menopause management is one of the most rewarding parts of primary care.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Illustration of a woman with heat symbols around her head and chest, moon/crescent for disrupted sleep, and thought bubbles showing frustration and confusion

content_chunks.title: The Menopause Transition: STRAW+10 Staging
content_chunks.content:
**STRAW+10 Staging System** (the standard):

• **Late Reproductive Stage**: Regular cycles, subtle FSH rise, declining fertility
• **Early Menopause Transition**: Variable cycle length (≥7 days difference from normal), elevated FSH
• **Late Menopause Transition**: ≥2 skipped cycles AND ≥1 interval of amenorrhea ≥60 days, FSH >25 IU/L
• **Early Menopause**: 12 months of amenorrhea (no other cause), FSH >40 IU/L
• **Late Menopause**: Begins 5 years after final menstrual period — urogenital symptoms dominant

**Perimenopause** = the transition period + first year after final period (3-8 years total)

**Key Symptoms**: Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats) — affect 75% of women. Sleep disturbance, mood changes, vaginal dryness, joint pain, brain fog.
content_chunks.mnemonic: **STRAW Stick**: **S**tage the transition: **T**racking cycles → **R**ising FSH → **A**menorrhea 60+ days → **W**hole year no period
content_chunks.visual_desc: Timeline graphic from late reproductive through late menopause with cycle patterns, FSH levels, and symptom prevalence shown along the continuum

content_chunks.title: Hormone Therapy: When, How, and For Whom
content_chunks.content:
**Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT) — Indications**:
• Moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats)
• Prevention of bone loss (in patients at high risk who can't take bisphosphonates)
• Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) — vaginal estrogen is FIRST-LINE

**The 'Window of Opportunity'**: Start MHT within **10 years of menopause** or age <60 for best risk-benefit ratio

**Regimens**:
| Patient Type | Regimen | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **With uterus** | Estrogen + Progestogen (protects endometrium) | Estradiol 0.5-1mg + micronized progesterone 100-200mg |
| **Without uterus** | Estrogen alone | Estradiol 0.5-1mg daily |
| **Vaginal symptoms only** | Low-dose vaginal estrogen | Estradiol vaginal cream/ring/tablet — minimal systemic absorption |

**Contraindications to MHT**:
❌ Breast cancer (current or history)
❌ Endometrial cancer
❌ Unexplained vaginal bleeding
❌ Active VTE or liver disease
❌ H/o coronary artery disease (if starting at age >60)

**Non-Hormonal Options for Hot Flashes**:
• **SSRI/SNRI**: Paroxetine 7.5mg (Brisdelle — FDA-approved!), venlafaxine 37.5-75mg
• **Gabapentin** 300-900mg (especially for nighttime hot flashes)
• **Oxybutynin** 2.5-5mg (emerging evidence)
• **Cognitive behavioral therapy** — reduces hot flash bother by 50%
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision matrix: Patient with vasomotor symptoms → Age/symptom severity → Uterus (yes/no) → Choose regimen → Reassess at 3 months then annually

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Vaginal estrogen is SAFE** — minimal systemic absorption, does NOT require progestogen protection, and is safe even for breast cancer survivors (though discuss with oncologist). Don't deny this to women with only urogenital symptoms just because they 'can't take systemic hormones.' Also: **Testosterone is NOT FDA-approved for low libido in women** — off-label use requires counseling on risks (acne, hirsutism, voice changes) and monitoring labs.

content_chunks.title: Perimenopause Workup
content_chunks.content:
**When to work up symptoms before attributing to menopause**:

✅ **TSH** — thyroid disease mimics menopause (fatigue, weight gain, mood changes)
✅ **FSH** (not diagnostic alone — fluctuates! But helpful if >25 in transition)
✅ **Pregnancy test** — always! Amenorrhea ≠ menopause until proven
✅ **CBC, iron panel** — heavy menstrual bleeding can cause iron deficiency
✅ **Lipid panel, glucose** — CV risk increases after menopause (estrogen withdrawal)
✅ **Bone density (DXA)** at menopause if risk factors: smoking, family h/o osteoporosis, BMI <20, steroid use
✅ **Mammogram** — up to date before starting MHT
content_chunks.visual_desc: Checklist-style infographic with a stethoscope, showing all screening items to rule out mimics before attributing symptoms to menopause

quick_checks.q: A 54-year-old woman with an intact uterus wants MHT for severe hot flashes. What's the BEST regimen?
quick_checks.explanation: Women with a uterus NEED progestogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from unopposed estrogen. Estrogen-only is for women s/p hysterectomy.

quick_checks.q: A 62-year-old breast cancer survivor has vaginal dryness and dyspareunia. What's the BEST option?
quick_checks.explanation: Vaginal estrogen has minimal systemic absorption. It's considered safe in most breast cancer survivors (though discuss with oncologist). Systemic estrogen is contraindicated in hormone-positive breast cancer.

lessons.title: 🔬 Vaginitis & Abnormal Pap: From Symptoms to Management

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Jasmine, 28, comes in embarrassed: 'I have this fishy smell and it's worse after sex. My partner says I'm fine but I'm so self-conscious.' She's tried OTC yeast treatments (Monistat × 3) with no improvement. She's worried something is 'seriously wrong.' Differentiating vaginitis types by history and office microscopy is a core FNP skill — treat the wrong thing and you make patients miserable (and waste their money on unnecessary OTC products).
content_chunks.visual_desc: Microscopy comparison images: clue cells (BV), pseudohyphae (yeast), trichomonads (trich) side by side with labeled features

content_chunks.title: The Big Three: BV, Candidiasis, Trichomoniasis
content_chunks.content:
**Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** — MOST common cause of abnormal discharge
• **Cause**: Replacement of lactobacilli by Gardnerella, Atopobium, etc.
• **Amsel's Criteria** (≥3 of 4 needed):
  1. Thin, gray-white, homogeneous discharge
  2. **Whiff test positive** (fishy odor with KOH)
  3. pH >4.5
  4. **Clue cells** on wet mount (>20% of epithelial cells)
• **Treatment**: Metronidazole 500mg BID ×7 days OR metronidazole gel 0.75% ×5 days
• **Nugent Score**: Gold standard Gram stain (0-10; ≥7 = BV)

**Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (VVC)**
• **Cause**: Candida albicans (90%), C. glabrata (resistant!)
• **Symptoms**: Thick, white, 'cottage cheese' discharge + pruritus + erythema
• **Diagnosis**: KOH wet mount → pseudohyphae visible
• **Treatment**: 
  - Uncomplicated: Fluconazole 150mg PO ×1 or OTC azole ×1-7 days
  - Complicated (recurrent, severe, non-albicans): Fluconazole 150mg q72h ×3 doses + maintenance ×6 months

**Trichomoniasis** — STI, MUST treat partner!
• **Cause**: Trichomonas vaginalis (flagellated protozoan)
• **Symptoms**: Frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge, strawberry cervix, dysuria
• **Diagnosis**: Wet mount → motile trichomonads (low sensitivity 60-70%); NAAT is gold standard
• **Treatment**: Metronidazole 2g PO ×1 OR Tinidazole 2g PO ×1
• **Key**: Treat partner! Screen for HIV and other STIs.
content_chunks.mnemonic: **VAGINAL**: **V**aginitis = **A**msel's (BV), **G**reen frothy (Trich), **I**tchy cottage cheese (Yeast), **N**-AAT for Trich, **A**zoles for yeast, **L**actobacillus repletion
content_chunks.visual_desc: Three-column comparison table: Discharge appearance, pH, KOH whiff test, microscopy findings, treatment for each condition

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Don't treat BV or Trich with just the patient — partners matter!** Trich requires partner treatment (metronidazole 2g ×1) or reinfection is guaranteed. BV: no clear benefit from routine partner treatment, but recommend condoms during treatment. **Also**: Fluconazole is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (high-dose linked to miscarriage). Use vaginal azoles instead for pregnant patients.

content_chunks.title: Abnormal Pap Smear: ASCCP 2019 Guidelines
content_chunks.content:
**Cervical Cancer Screening Schedule** (USPSTF/ACOG):
• Age 21-29: Pap alone q3 years
• Age 30-65: Pap + HPV co-testing q5 years (preferred) OR Pap alone q3 years
• Age >65: Discontinue if adequate negative prior screening

**Interpreting Results**:

| Result | Next Step |
|---|---|
| **NILM** (negative) | Routine screening |
| **ASC-US** + HPV neg | Routine screening (co-test) or repeat Pap in 1yr (cytology alone) |
| **ASC-US** + HPV pos | **Colposcopy** |
| **LSIL** | Colposcopy (or reflex HPV triage if cotesting shows HPV+) |
| **ASC-H** | Colposcopy + endocervical sampling |
| **HSIL** | Colposcopy + endocervical sampling → risk of CIN2+ is high |
| **AGC** (atypical glandular) | Colposcopy + endocervical sampling + endometrial biopsy (if >35 or bleeding) |

**Management of CIN**:
• **CIN 1** (mild dysplasia): Observation if ASC-US/LSIL and colposcopy adequate (80% regress in 2 years)
• **CIN 2/3**: Excision (LEEP, cold knife cone) — do not observe unless pregnant or special circumstances
• **HPV 16/18**: Higher risk of progression — more aggressive follow-up

**HPV Vaccine**: Gardasil-9 covers 9 high-risk types. Recommended ages 9-26 (catch-up 27-45 with shared decision-making). Prevents 90% of cervical cancers!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Algorithm flowchart from Pap result → ASC-US/LSIL/ASC-H/HSIL/AGC → Colposcopy vs follow-up timing → Management by pathology result

quick_checks.q: A 32-year-old has frothy yellow-green discharge, pH 6.0, and a strawberry cervix. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Frothy yellow-green discharge, elevated pH, and strawberry cervix (petechiae) are classic for Trichomonas vaginalis. Confirm with NAAT and treat with metronidazole 2g PO ×1.

quick_checks.q: A 35-year-old patient has ASC-US on Pap with positive high-risk HPV. Next step?
quick_checks.explanation: Per ASCCP 2019 guidelines: ASC-US + HPV positive → colposcopy. LEEP is treatment for CIN2+, not the initial diagnostic step.
